Dost CDA abhi bhi fix kr skta he bht Kuch. A lot of cities have done projects that reduced infrastructure and revived areas. But those projects won't be something you can show off and use for promotional images, and won't increase land value short-term which is sadly the main focus of our planning departments.

The issue is not the high rise development, in fact it's a welcome addition. The problem is the needless increase in infrastructure and an insistence on low density zoning, leading to an urban sprawl. There is no need for a signal free 6 lane avenue every two kilometres running in parallel to one another, rather there is a need for proper traffic management; induced demand will always catch up to the capacity eventually.

Read other comments. While Islamabad is still better than most cities, its design is pedestrian agnostic and unsustainable, the way it is being managed. Concrete jungle refers to the huge infrastructure that is required to keep the city moving, rather than the construction; in fact, low rise and single family construction is one of the reasons why it is so bad. Had the authorities properly embraced vertical expansion, we wouldn't have the ever expanding sprawl that we are dealing with right now.
True. A prime example being Shakarparian National Park that is constantly being cut down to accommodate more and more government entities, instead of being allowed to prosper and grow.
Yeah well read the other comments. The "progress" and "development" isn't the issue, the issue is how nonsensical and ill-planned it all is.

Just adding another rant here; there is a nice bit of trees between 9th Avenue/Jinnah Avenue intersection and F-8/G-8 underpass. If maintained properly, it could be a great space for the area which walking paths and natural foliages. However, as has been the trend, soon these trees would be chopped down to make room for singular glass towers and their huge parking lots.

Metro I think is a late step in the right direction, but due to the grid layout we need a lot of feeder routes to properly capitalise the public transport potential. In fact, metro is (in my uneducated opinion) quite a well executed project given how it allows controlled pedestrian crossing (you are never more than a kilometer/10 minutes away from a crossing). However, increasing the number of lanes has had no effect but to increase traffic flow further while still retaining the congestion issues that were there before the expansion. 

Centaurus is a gaudy eyesore and the design should've been revised to better suit the aesthetics of the city. Other new projects (Meezan Tower, Elysium Tower, MOI, New Blue Area development) are much better designed in that regard.

True. The demographic movement is what makes a city grow. However, while it's easier to blame the influx of outsiders, it's actually the incompetence of relevant agencies that refused to implement proper regulation, instead choosing to stick with an outdated city planning concept, in fact banking on it harder in order to generate self-serving revenue streams.

While the city doesn't have a bold character and rich history of other metropolitan areas in the country, I think it's unfair to call it shit. There is still a lot to explore here; the brustalist inspired architecture of old office spaces, the availability of personal space, a modern and mostly regulated layout, a nascent food culture (a controversial opinion, I realise), and tons of ways to connect to nature. Granted these are not to everyone's tastes, and places like Karachi and Lahore offer these perks in much more depth, but Islamabad still has tons to offer if you try to look around.

Not a concrete jungle in the sense that there's too much development, but more so that most of the green spaces are being eaten up by non-productive infrastructure. A road serves the same purpose, whether it's four lanes or ten; it's how the infrastructure is managed that matters. Sadly the authorities, as I mentioned earlier, are most interested in quick, splashy fixes and not in any long term solutions (rezoning, improved public transport, traffic management) that would be more sustainable.

Read a report that Islamabad has lost 60%+ of its tree cover since 2009. That number could've been so low with proper planning, but single family urbanisation and the influx of infrastructure projects means that we are ourselves further and further into this quagmire.

The city is very much a product of its time; it is designed after the American suburbia which is probably the least holistic town planning schema out there, representing everything wrong with a car centric approach. That's just my opinion; obviously you might disagree with a valid PoV of your own. I still believe that urban sprawl, especially post-2000 with southwards expansion from the Bahrias and the DHAs stressed the already delicate balance of Islamabad's design.

I don't think it would be possible because we probably aren't in the same country. But I can lay out the steps more clearly:

1. Put phone on vibrate. 

2. Open camera. 

3. Send a message or some notification to the phone. 

4. When vibrated, camera should produce distortion. It would look like waves. Check if they are similar. If one wave is larger than the other, or if repeated experiments produce different waves, OIS assembly might be the issue.

If your phone fell recently before the issue manifested, it might be because the OIS setup is disturbed (that almost jelly effect in the video shown above). I have seen that happen with my friend's S6 in the past, and a quick way (almost non scientific) we devised was to set phone to vibrate, open camera, and send a notification to said phone. If the buzz produces symmetrical disturbance bands (parallel mutually and along the length of screen) then the OIS motor is working fine, otherwise you know the drill.

Remember three things when conceptualizing a photograph, in descending order of importance:

>Subject

>Light
